short_cite: Lalit, Ramachandran & Mishra (1986), coal power in India
full_citation: Lalit, B.Y., Ramachandran, T.V. and Mishra, U.C. (1986). Radiation exposures due to coal-fired power stations in India. Radiation Protection Dosimetry 15(3): 197-202. Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Bombay.
notes: READ (staged scan lalit1986.pdf, 6 pp; text layer empty, so read from page images at 110-220 dpi). 29 Indian stations, 10,102 MWe installed (36 table rows because 7 stations appear twice at different capacities: the later row supersedes), sampling 1976-83. Table 1: installed capacity, plant load factor, coal t/d per MW, ash %, Ra-226/Th-228/K-40 in fly ash. Table 2: coal activity (Ra-226 14.8-51.9 Bq/kg). Table 3: modelled annual airborne release in MBq/y per station (Ra-226, Th-228, K-40). Releases are MODELLED (McBride et al. 1977 method; text assumes 97% fly-ash control for ESP stations and 82% for mechanical collectors), not stack measurements; Table 3 implies a uniform 3.0% of ash-borne Ra-226 for every station including the asterisked mechanical-collector stations (internal inconsistency, see benchmarks.md). 1,800 MWe of 10,100 MWe (17.8%) had mechanical collectors only. Article DOI not verified; URL is the journal issue page.

short_cite: Bem et al. (2002), Lodz region coal plants
full_citation: Bem, H., Wieczorkowski, P. and Budzanowski, M. (2002). Evaluation of technologically enhanced natural radiation near the coal-fired power plants in the Lodz region of Poland. Journal of Environmental Radioactivity 61(2): 191-201.
notes: READ (staged bem2002.pdf, 11 pp). Lodz region: total dust 8,210 Mg (1996), of which three power stations 3,055 Mg; earlier decades 45,000 Mg (1980) falling to 30,350 Mg (1990), about 100,000 Mg/y in 1960-64; one central plant had <90% ash removal until 1995; modern plants >99.5%. Annual atmospheric discharge (1996-97, all Lodz coal burning): U-238 1.1, Ra-226 0.8, Pb-210 1.2, Th-232 0.6, K-40 5.3 GBq, computed from captured fly-ash concentrations (Ra-226 86-104, Pb-210 112-183 Bq/kg), i.e. no extra volatile enrichment assumed. No electricity output given, so NOT convertible to TBq per GW.a. Article DOI not verified; URL is the journal issue page.

short_cite: Pandit, Sahu & Puranik (2011), Indian coal plant atmospheric release
full_citation: Pandit, G.G., Sahu, S.K. and Puranik, V.D. (2011). Natural radionuclides from coal fired thermal power plants: estimation of atmospheric release and inhalation risk. Radioprotection 46(6): S173-S179 (ICRER 2011).
notes: READ via the fetch tool (verbatim extraction of the model-plant paragraph and Table 1; direct curl download returned HTTP 403, so the PDF itself was not opened). Model 1000 MWe plant, 12.5 t coal per MW per day (12,500 t/d), 20% of ash as bottom ash and 80% as fly ash, ESP assumed 99% efficient, stack fly ash 0.46 kg/s. Table 1 (Bq/s): Ra-226 18.7-69.8 (35.7), Th-228 43.7-106 (57.9), Pb-210 11.8-32.0 (18.6), U-238 8.6-55.8 (27.7); fly-ash concentrations from three Indian plants (not named, no year). Emission is MODELLED from an assumed ESP efficiency, not measured. Capacity factor not stated (treated as 1.0 here). No UNSCEAR comparison of the emission rates in the paper.

full_citation: Gabbard, A. (1993). Coal Combustion: Nuclear Resource or Danger? ORNL Review 26(3-4), Oak Ridge National Laboratory (web-archived copy printed 2008, hosted by US NRC as ML083260701).
notes: READ via the fetch tool (summary extraction, PDF not opened directly). The ORNL URL https://www.ornl.gov/info/ornlreview/rev26-34/text/colmain.html failed to fetch. This is the Gabbard ORNL item found; the report number ORNL/TM-12180 given in the task brief could NOT be verified and may be a different document. Typical 1000 MWe US plant: about 4 million short tons coal per year (3.63 Mt), U 1.3 ppm and Th 3.2 ppm (EPA 1984 figures), 5.2 short tons U and 12.8 short tons Th per plant-year, precipitators about 99.5% efficient, about 1% of uranium escapes with fly ash (NCRP). The article's per-plant 'released' figures equal the whole content of the coal burned (input inventory, not emission) and are internally inconsistent with the 1% escape statement. Secondary compilation of EPA/NCRP/McBride inputs; treat as a composition and tonnage cross-check only.

full_citation: Nicol, K. (2013). Recent developments in particulate control. IEA Clean Coal Centre report CCC/218, London, March 2013. ISBN 978-92-9029-538-9.
notes: READ (downloaded, text extracted; relevant passages sections 2.2 and 3). Global fleet: about 2,500 pulverised-coal plants worldwide, 95% of them with some particulate control, about 80% of which is cold-side ESP (so about 1,800 plants); ESP is 85% of installed particulate-control fleet in Germany and 80% in the USA (Li et al. 2011; Seyfert 2011); ESP efficiencies 98-99.8%; historical ESP efficiency about 80% on some units when coal changed. Snapshot circa 2012; no time series.

short_cite: IEA CCC CCC/231 (Zhang 2014), coal combustion wastes
full_citation: Zhang, X. (2014). Management of coal combustion wastes. IEA Clean Coal Centre report CCC/231, London, January 2014. ISBN 978-92-9029-551-8.
notes: READ (downloaded; abstract, introduction and Table 1). World coal combustion products (CCPs) about 780 Mt in 2010 (Feuerborn 2012; Heidrich et al. 2013), about 53% utilised. Table 1 (2010): China 400 Mt, India 123.5, USA 118.1, EU-15 48, Russia 26.6, Poland 19.6, Australia 14.1, Japan 10.7, Korea 8.41. CCPs include fly ash, bottom ash, boiler slag and FGD gypsum, and some non-power ash, so the figure exceeds power-station ash alone.
